summary_md: **Rohan Paul ([@rohanpaul_ai](https://x.com/rohanpaul_ai/status/2115898609304801525))** summarizes a Princeton–Meta paper, *Don't Forget What You Just Learned* ([arXiv 2610.31846](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31846)): with Self-Direction, a failing agent reflects and trains the lesson into a tiny LoRA adapter (~0.02% of the model), and a router loads the nearest adapter on similar tasks; with Qwen3.6-27B, GAIA success rose from 38.8% to 55.8%, beating in-context reflections and a Skills.md file.

media.ocr_text:
Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed
Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons
Yuval Kansall,2,*, Karen Ullrich?, Polina Kirichenko?, Ilia Kulikov?, Niraj K. Jha', Mohammad Pezeshki?,
Mark Ibrahim?
1Princeton University, 2Meta FAIR
*Work done during an internship at Meta FAIR.
Intelligent agents should learn from their mistakes so that experience leads to continuous improvement.
Yet today's agents recover from a mistake only temporarily: in-context reflections are easily forgotten
across sessions and compete for limited context, while full-parameter fine-tuning is expensive and can
22 Oct 2026
interfere with existing capabilities. We introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn
from mistakes that combines the benefits of temporary in-context retries and policy updates. When
an agent fails a task, it reflects on its own trajectory in order to extract a lesson and immediately
distills it into a lightweight low-rank adapter. By keeping the original weights frozen, Self-Direction
prevents adapter training from overwriting base-model parameters while training additional parameters
equivalent to ~ 0.02% of the base model's parameter count for each adapter. The agent then saves
these adapters in a persistent library of lessons, automatically routing them to solve related problems
later. Experiments with agents based on open-weight models from the Qwen family across open-ended
research (GAIA), tool-use workflows (Claw-Eval), and terminal tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1) show that
0.31846v1 [cs.AI]
our method improves overall success rates by 8.9 to 17.0 percentage points and performs competitively
with frontier systems. We find that Self-Direction reduces repeated mistakes across future encounters
of a task, nearly doubling the reliability of an agent's corrections. Learned lessons also transfer: a
handful of adapters generalize to dozens of new tasks without additional training. Ultimately, this
self-directed repair transforms everyday mistakes into lasting lessons.
